name: Project Management Plan
purpose: The plan describes how the team will execute, monitor, control and close the project. Besides a little unique content it is mostly the subsidiary management plans and the baselines, combined into one integrated approach. It is developed during initial planning and usually changes only after a significant change in the charter, environment or scope.

elements.guidance: Describe the life cycle used to do the project: the name of each phase, its key activities, key deliverables, entry criteria, exit criteria and key reviews. The blank form prints two tables: Phase with Key Activities and Key Deliverables, and Phase with Reviews, Entry Criteria and Exit Criteria.

Document how each key deliverable will be created. Common approaches are predictive (scope known and stable) and adaptive (scope evolving and subject to change); iterative or incremental development may also be named.
List the subsidiary plans that are part of this plan, as a table of contents, links to electronic copies, or a list of separate documents that count as part of it.

Define which scope variances are acceptable, which are a warning and which are unacceptable. Scope variance can be expressed by the features and functions present in the end product or by the performance metrics wanted.

Describe how the scope baseline is managed, including the response to acceptable, warning and unacceptable variance; what triggers preventive or corrective action; and when the change control process is used. Define the difference between a scope revision and a scope change (the book's example: changing a color is a revision, changing a function is a change).
Define acceptable, warning and unacceptable schedule variance. It may be a percent of variance from the baseline, or the amount of float used, or whether any schedule reserve has been used.
Describe how the schedule baseline is managed: responses to acceptable, warning and unacceptable variance, what triggers preventive or corrective action, and when change control is enacted.
Define acceptable, warning and unacceptable cost variance. It may be a percent of variance from the baseline; the book's example bands are 0 to 5 percent, 5 to 10 percent and greater than 10 percent.
Describe how the cost baseline is managed: responses to acceptable, warning and unacceptable variance, what triggers preventive or corrective action, and when change control is enacted.

tailoring: On a large and complex project each subsidiary plan will likely be a stand-alone plan; present the project management plan as a shell with only the life cycle, development approach and key reviews, and link or refer to the detailed subsidiary plans.
On a smaller project, a project roadmap that summarizes phases, major deliverables, milestones and key reviews may be enough.
Expect additional subsidiary plans that fit the nature of the project, such as a technology, logistics or safety management plan.
agile_or_adaptive: Table 2.1 names adaptive approaches (scope evolving and subject to change) next to predictive ones for the Development approaches element, and adds iterative and incremental development. The book gives no other adaptive-specific guidance for this form.
